editorial.headline: Fruit Retail, Nationally Open but Closed to PMA Registration in Bali
editorial.standfirst: This specialised fruit-retail activity is nationally open to full foreign ownership, but Bali’s permanent moratorium blocks PMA registration for it.
editorial.body:
A foreign investor cannot register this specialised fruit-retail activity in Bali today. The activity is the retail sale of fruit as a distinct line of trade, encompassing fruit such as apples, grapes, avocados, star fruit, duku, durian, guava, citrus, mangoes, mangosteens, pineapples, bananas, papayas, rambutan, sapodilla, salak and watermelon. Its commercial identity is therefore precise: a business registered for fruit retail, rather than a broader description assembled from assumptions about how it may operate.

Nationally, the position is open. Foreign ownership may reach 100%, under the stated presidential-regulation source. The activity is also open across the Micro, Small, Medium and Large scales. That combination matters because it gives the national record a clear shape: this is not an activity reserved from foreign investment at the national level, nor is access confined to one stated business scale. A prospective registrant can see both the specialised retail scope and the full set of scales expressly open to it.

Bali changes the practical answer for PMA registration. At the Large scale, the OSS risk classification is Low or Medium-Low across every scope, and the provincial moratorium blocks PMA registration on that basis. The moratorium applies island-wide and permanently to all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI activities for PMA. National openness does not translate into a PMA registration route in Bali for this activity. The distinction is not a minor local qualification: it determines whether a foreign-owned vehicle can register the activity in the province at all.

For founders, the disciplined reading is to keep the two levels separate. The national record permits up to full foreign ownership and recognises the activity at every listed scale. Bali’s rule nevertheless blocks PMA registration because of the relevant risk classification and the provincial moratorium. Both statements are true at once, and neither should be used to soften or overstate the other.
